hints: In postorder, the root is written last. If you read postorder from the back, which subtree do you meet first?
Use divide and conquer on inorder ranges with a value→index HashMap. Use a pointer that moves backward through postorder, and build the right subtree before the left.

1. Map each inorder value to its index.
  2. Set ptr = n−1, the last index of postorder.
  3. build(lo, hi): if lo > hi, return null.
  4. Take postorder[ptr--] as the root and find its index m in inorder.
  5. Build the right child from (m+1, hi) first, then the left child from (lo, m−1).

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Find the root in inorder with a linear scan and recurse on copied subarrays.

approaches.name: Optimal (index map + backward pointer)
approaches.idea: Look up each split in O(1) and read postorder from the end, building the right subtree before the left.

explain: Postorder [1,3,2,7,4] ends with 4, so 4 is the root. It sits at index 3 of inorder [1,2,3,4,7]. Reading backward, the next value is 7, which is the root of the right part [7]. Then comes 2, the root of the left part [1,2,3], followed by its right child 3 and left child 1. The result is [4,2,7,1,3]. Building the left subtree first would take the wrong values, because reversed postorder visits node, right, then left.
recognize: When you get inorder plus postorder, the root is the last postorder value, and inorder splits the left and right subtrees.
